opus-5.5.text:
Weather was a real eye-opener for us, because it's the poster child of a problem where people had assumed you needed massive physics-based simulations running on supercomputers. Numerical weather prediction is one of the great scientific achievements of the last century, but it's incredibly expensive. You're solving these coupled fluid dynamics equations at fine resolution, and every forecast eats up a huge amount of compute.

When we built FourCastNet, which used a Fourier neural operator-based architecture, the first thing that struck me was the speed-up: orders of magnitude faster than traditional models at inference time, while getting competitive accuracy on many key variables. That changes what you can do. You're no longer limited to a handful of ensemble members. You can run thousands of them, and that matters enormously for extreme events like hurricanes or heat waves, where the tail of the distribution is what you care about.

But the deeper lesson for me was about why neural operators work there. Weather is fundamentally a continuous phenomenon. The atmosphere doesn't live on a grid; the grid is just an artifact of how we discretize it. Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, so they capture the underlying physics in a way that's resolution-agnostic. You can train at one resolution and evaluate at another, which a standard convolutional network or transformer on fixed pixels just can't do in a principled way. Working in the Fourier domain also handles the global, multi-scale structure of atmospheric flows really naturally.

It also taught me some humility. Purely data-driven models can drift on long rollouts, and they can produce things that look plausible but violate conservation laws. That's pushed us toward incorporating physics more explicitly, with physics-informed losses, constraints, and hybrid approaches, so you get both the speed of learning and the reliability of the equations.

So the big takeaway was that this isn't just a faster weather model. It's evidence that AI can become a genuine tool for scientific simulation broadly: climate, fluid dynamics, materials, plasma physics, anywhere you have expensive PDEs. Weather was the proof point that convinced a lot of skeptics, including some in the traditional modeling community, that this direction is real.

r001.rationale: The response discusses applications to areas with expensive PDEs, but does not say neural operators can be used without assuming the system is governed by PDEs.

r002.rationale: It says FourCastNet achieved “competitive accuracy on many key variables” compared with traditional models.

r003.rationale: It says inference was “orders of magnitude faster,” but does not specify tens of thousands of times faster.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute others’ ability to build on the model to a permissive open-source release.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Weather forecasting was really the moment where neural operators went from being a beautiful mathematical idea to something I could point at and say, this changes how we do science.

The core idea of a neural operator is that instead of learning a map from one fixed grid of numbers to another, you learn a map between functions. The atmosphere is a continuous field. Temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, these exist at every point in space, not just at the grid points where we happen to have data. Traditional neural networks are tied to a resolution. Train them at one resolution and they are stuck there. Neural operators, and the Fourier neural operator in particular, learn in function space, so you can train at one resolution and query at another. That property turned out to be exactly what weather needed.

When we built FourCastNet with NVIDIA and collaborators, the first thing that struck me was speed. The numerical weather prediction systems that agencies run are enormous. They solve the Navier-Stokes equations on supercomputers, and a single forecast takes hours on thousands of CPUs. FourCastNet was producing a global forecast in a fraction of a second on a single GPU. That is four or five orders of magnitude faster. And the accuracy was competitive with the operational systems on many variables at short to medium range.

The lesson there was not just "faster is nice." It was that speed unlocks a qualitatively different kind of forecasting. If a forecast is essentially free, you can run thousands of them. You can do large ensembles that actually capture the uncertainty in extreme events, hurricanes, atmospheric rivers, heat waves. The tail risks are what actually matter for people, and the traditional systems could only afford ensembles of fifty members or so. We could do thousands. That reframed what the model was for.

The second lesson was about data and physics working together rather than against each other. A lot of people assumed the physics-based community and the machine learning community were on opposite sides. But what we saw is that the neural operator learns from decades of reanalysis data, which itself is a blend of observations and physical models. The learned model is implicitly absorbing physics. And where you do want to constrain it, you can. You can add physics-informed losses, you can enforce conservation properties. So the framing shifted from replacing physics to accelerating and augmenting it.

The third thing it taught me was humility about generalization. The atmosphere is chaotic, and errors compound as you roll a forecast forward. Early versions blurred out fine structure at longer lead times. That pushed us toward better architectures, spherical harmonics instead of planar Fourier transforms so the model respects the geometry of the globe, and toward thinking carefully about how you train autoregressively. Those failure modes were instructive. They told us where the mathematics still needed to meet the application.

And honestly, the biggest takeaway was that weather was a proof of concept for something much broader. The same operator-learning framework now does carbon capture simulation, plasma modeling for fusion, fluid dynamics for aircraft design, even medical device design. All of these are problems governed by partial differential equations where the traditional simulation is the bottleneck. Weather showed us that if you can learn the solution operator once, you can collapse that bottleneck across all of them. It convinced me that neural operators are not a niche trick for one domain. They are a general tool for scientific computing in the way that convolutional networks became a general tool for vision.

r002.rationale: It says FourCastNet's accuracy was “competitive with the operational systems” on many variables at short to medium range.

r003.rationale: It says forecasts took a fraction of a second rather than hours and were four or five orders of magnitude faster, which covers tens of thousands of times.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention an open-source release or attribute others’ ability to build on the model to one.

astra-6.text:
Weather forecasting really showed me the potential of neural operators to learn complex dynamics at scale. You’re predicting how an entire field evolves—temperature, pressure, wind—not just assigning a label to an input. That’s a natural setting for learning an operator that maps one function to another.

What’s exciting is what speed makes possible. If you can generate forecasts much faster, you can run many more scenarios and get a better picture of uncertainty. That matters because a single forecast doesn’t tell you the whole story, especially when you’re concerned about extreme events.

But it also reinforces that accuracy on average isn’t enough. You need to examine rare events, long-term stability, and whether the predictions respect the underlying physics. For me, the potential is in bringing learning and scientific modeling together, and extending that approach to other physical systems.

sol-6.1.text:
Weather forecasting showed me that neural operators could tackle complex, multiscale systems at a level that was practically useful. You’re learning how an entire physical field evolves, rather than predicting a single number. With FourCastNet, we saw that this approach could produce forecasts remarkably quickly while capturing a lot of the structure of the atmosphere.

That speed opens up something very important: ensembles. You want many possible forecasts so you can understand uncertainty and assess the risk of extreme events. If each forecast is much cheaper, you can explore many more possibilities.

For me, the broader lesson was that neural operators could become a powerful tool for scientific simulation. But speed alone isn’t enough. You still have to ask whether the model captures the physics, how it behaves over long rollouts, and whether it can handle rare events.
